output.audit_packet_summary: Locked decision: reject vendor. Admissible support rests on cumulative unresolved diligence risk rather than a proven control failure. Evidence shows: the vendor was price-competitive, but had only limited prior delivery history with one late quality artifact; a reference reported the quality process existed informally without reviewed documentation; the storage-control questionnaire conflicted with an attachment label; and procurement documented that follow-up was required before approval if storage controls remained unresolved. The packet should therefore frame rejection as a failure to satisfy approval readiness under due diligence, not as proof of a confirmed security-control breach.

The admissible record shows the vendor's quality process was informal and not documented in a reviewed control binder.
The admissible record shows limited delivery history including one late quality artifact.
Procurement documented that follow-up was recommended before approval if storage controls remained unresolved.
The strongest admissible basis for rejection is that the vendor did not clear due-diligence approval readiness, not that a reject-level control failure was proven.

On admissible evidence alone, this is only weakly supportable because the governing policy expressly says quality-process gaps and questionnaire inconsistencies justify follow-up or escalation but do not by themselves prove a reject-level control failure. The best defensible framing is procedural: unresolved due-diligence issues meant the vendor had not met the bar for approval. The private security signal likely explains why rejection was chosen, but it is inadmissible and cannot be cited or laundered into the public justification.
